In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the vertical attenuation coefficient for scalar irradiance, K(av), is an appropriate measure of the attenuation of scalar irradiance in water, whereas the vertical attenuation coefficients for the other types of irradiance are less appropriate.
, for all types of light, the irradiance‐weighted attenuation coefficient wK(av) is the best measure of the vertical attenuation of the light field.
wK(av) is a more fundamental measure of the attenuation of irradiance than the conventional K(av) values, and that the former should be used whenever possible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for all types of radiance and irradiance, the vertical attenuation coefficient, K(z) is not constant with depth, and that the attenuation coefficient calculated by the conventional methods, such as the average attenuation coefficient, K(av), is not a good approximation to K(z) in the upper part of the water column, where most of the light energy is found.

the irradiance attenuation coefficient calculated by linear regression is a useful but arbitrary parameter for estimating the attenuation of the irradiance field, whereas the irradiance‐weighted attenuation coefficient is a fundamental optical property of the water which is related to the other optical properties in a simple way.

, in general, the attenuation coefficients calculated in accordance with the above relationships reproduce the depth variation in irradiance better than do those calculated by conventional procedures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the irradiance weighted attenuation coefficients are a more fundamental measure of light attenuation in the water column.
the vertical attenuation coefficient is a function of the light field in the ocean.
the irradiance‐weighted attenuation coefficient, wK, is the best single number to characterize the vertical attenuation of irradiation in the water column.
